# Model Architecture and Encoding

Also called: NeRF Architectures, Coordinate Encoding Schemes, Radiance Field Representations

## Overview
This family defines the neural network structures and coordinate encoding functions that map 3D spatial coordinates and viewing directions to volume density and color. It solves the problem of representing continuous 3D radiance fields with sufficient frequency detail to capture high-frequency geometry and view-dependent appearance, while managing computational cost and memory usage. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its focus on the internal representation of the scene (MLPs, grids, tensors) and the mathematical transformation of input coordinates (positional encoding, hash encoding, frequency modulation), rather than the optimization loop or loss functions.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family map an input coordinate $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and a viewing direction $\mathbf{d} \in S^2$ to a volume density $\sigma \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ and an RGB color vector $\mathbf{c} \in [0, 1]^3$. The core mechanism involves:
1.  **Coordinate Encoding:** Transforming raw coordinates into a higher-dimensional feature space using basis functions (e.g., sinusoidal, hash-based, or learned) to help the network resolve high-frequency details.
2.  **Feature Aggregation:** Combining features from the coordinate encoding with scene-specific parameters (e.g., grid values, latent codes, or tensor components).
3.  **Network Decoding:** Passing the aggregated features through a neural network (typically a Multi-Layer Perceptron or MLP) to predict density and color.

## Subtopics

### [Depth-Guided NeRF Training Configuration](11916-depth-guided-nerf-training-configuration.md)
This configuration modifies the standard NeRF architecture by inserting dropout layers with probability $p=0.1$ after each of the first eight fully connected ReLU-activated layers that encode the positional encoding. It is distinguished from siblings by its specific use of Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) for depth alignment and a fixed dropout regularization scheme on the positional encoding layers, rather than relying on semantic guidance or binary occupancy. Choose this method when explicit depth supervision is required to resolve geometric ambiguity in standard NeRF training.

### [CLIPNeRF Training Configuration](12073-clipnerf-training-configuration.md)
This configuration freezes the density parameters of the NeRF and utilizes a directional loss that enforces semantic alignment with text embeddings in the CLIP space, rather than photometric fidelity. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF reconstruction by optimizing only the color/feature fields to match text prompts, using a patch-based rendering approach ($128 \times 128$) to manage memory. Choose this method for text-guided stylization of NeRFs.

### [Binary Radiance Fields](13622-binary-radiance-fields.md)
Binary Radiance Fields (BiRF) constrains feature encoding parameters in multi-resolution hash grids to binary values $\{-1, +1\}$, reducing storage overhead to approximately 0.5 MB for standard scenes. Unlike post-processing compression methods, BiRF performs binarization during training using a straight-through estimator, allowing end-to-end optimization. It employs a 2D-3D hybrid multi-resolution architecture (one 3D voxel grid and three 2D plane grids) to mitigate hash collisions. Choose this method when storage efficiency is critical and end-to-end training is preferred over post-hoc compression.

### [Mip-NeRF 360 MLP Architecture](14098-mip-nerf-360-mlp-architecture.md)
The Mip-NeRF 360 MLP architecture replaces standard positional encoding with **Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE)** to handle aliasing and frequency uncertainty by integrating over conical frustums defined by covariance lifting. It structures the model into a density network (8 layers, 256 width) and a color network (1 layer, 128 width) with specific skip connections and bias configurations. It is distinguished from standard NeRF by its explicit handling of spatial extent via covariance lifting and from later grid-based methods by its reliance on dense MLP layers. Choose this method for anti-aliased rendering of unbounded scenes.

### [SUDS](14964-suds.md)
SUDS is a 4D radiance field representation that factorizes the scene into three separate multi-resolution hash table structures: static, dynamic, and far-field. It enables free-viewpoint rendering and 3D scene flow estimation at arbitrary poses and time steps using only unlabeled inputs. Unlike sibling methods that rely on supervised 3D bounding boxes, SUDS achieves scalability to hundreds of square kilometers by combining spatial partitioning with video-specific hash indexing. Choose this method for large-scale dynamic urban scene reconstruction.

### [CCNeRF](15008-ccnerf.md)
CCNeRF models the radiance field as a hybrid tensor rank decomposition (CP and Triple Plane), eliminating the need for neural networks during rendering. Unlike NeRF variants that rely on shared MLP renderers, CCNeRF uses only tensor rank decomposition, preserving low-rank approximation properties to allow dynamic model size adjustment via rank truncation and composition via rank concatenation without retraining. Choose this method for efficient compression and arbitrary composition of 3D scenes.

### [Rip-NeRF](15532-rip-nerf.md)
Rip-NeRF renders high-fidelity, anti-aliased images by combining cone casting with an anisotropic 3D Gaussian representation encoded via Platonic Solid Projection and Ripmap Encoding. It differs from sibling methods like Zip-NeRF by replacing inefficient multi-sampling mechanisms with compact, learnable Ripmap features on Platonic solid faces, enabling efficient anisotropic area-sampling. Choose this method for high-quality anti-aliased rendering of complex geometries.

### [UE4-NeRF](15539-ue4-nerf.md)
UE4-NeRF partitions the environment into sub-NeRFs represented as textured polygonal meshes and integrates them into the Unreal Engine 4 (UE4) rasterization pipeline. Unlike Block-NeRF which is limited to grid structures, UE4-NeRF uses regular octahedra for mesh initialization and stores opacity in texture maps to handle complex outdoor environments. It achieves real-time performance by leveraging multi-resolution hash encoding for training acceleration and a Level of Detail (LOD) hierarchy for rendering. Choose this method for real-time interactive rendering of large-scale 3D scenes.

### [Generative Occupancy Fields (GOF)](15773-generative-occupancy-fields-gof.md)
Generative Occupancy Fields (GOF) combines radiance fields with occupancy representations to learn compact object surfaces without impeding training convergence. Unlike its siblings, GOF predicts alpha values (interpreted as occupancy) instead of volume densities, enabling surface-aware image synthesis via root-finding. Choose this method for 3D-aware image synthesis where sharp surfaces are required.

### [Panoptic Radiance Field](15849-panoptic-radiance-field.md)
Panoptic Lifting learns a panoptic 3D volumetric representation from posed RGB images and machine-generated 2D panoptic segmentation masks, lifting noisy 2D labels into a consistent 3D representation comprising color, density, semantics, and instances. It differs from siblings like Panoptic NeRF by requiring only machine-generated 2D labels rather than manual ground truth or coarse meshes, and from SemanticNeRF by explicitly modeling 3D-consistent instance identifiers via surrogate IDs. Choose this method for panoptic 3D scene understanding from 2D labels.

### [Frequency-Modulated Position Encoding](15897-frequency-modulated-position-encoding.md)
Frequency-Modulated Position Encoding maps 3D spatial coordinates and viewing directions to feature vectors using sine and cosine basis functions with exponentially spaced frequencies. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF positional encoding by narrowing the encoding interval and using specific frequency bands ($L=10$ for space, $L=2$ for direction) tailored for point cloud rasterization, which compensates for sparsity and enables efficient editing. Choose this method for point-based differentiable volume rendering.

### Triplane NeRF with Diffusion Prior
- **Definition:** The framework uses a triplane NeRF representation where scene codes are optimized jointly with a diffusion prior to handle sparse-view data and ensure end-to-end coherence [S1].
- **Parameters:** Prediction Format uses v-parameterization $\hat{v}_\phi(x(t), t)$ from [43], such that $\hat{x} = \alpha(t)x(t) - \sigma(t)\hat{v}$. Weighting Function $w(t)$ uses SNR-based weighting $w(t) = (\alpha(t)/\sigma(t))^{2\omega}$ from Eq. (5), instead of LSGM mechanisms [S1].
- **Layout:** Scene code $\xi_i$ has shape $\mathbb{R}^{3 \times 6 \times 128 \times 128}$, representing a triplane NeRF representation. The Denoising Network is a U-Net with 122M parameters, taking noisy and denoised triplane features as input/output, with channels of all three planes stacked together [S1].

### EG3D Triplane Representation
- **Steps:** Render feature image $I_f \in \mathbb{R}^{32 \times 128 \times 128}$ and raw RGB image $I_{128} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 128 \times 128}$ by accumulating points along rays and performing volume rendering. Extract dense depth map $I_D \in \mathbb{R}^{128 \times 128}$ from the volume rendering. Feed $I_f$ and $I_{128}$ into a 2D super-resolution network to yield final output $I_{512} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 512 \times 512}$ [S2].
- **Formula:** $\text{SuperRes}(I_f, I_{128}) = I_{512}$ [S2].
- **Parameters:** Image resolution is 512x512 for input images and final output [S2].
- **Layout:** Triplane representation $T$ is a tensor in $\mathbb{R}^{256 \times 256 \times 96}$, corresponding to 3 axis-aligned planes (xy, xz, yz), each with 32 channels and resolution 256x256 [S2].
- **Number:** Rendering speed is 42 fps on RTX 3090 [S2].

### NeRF-W Hyperparameter Configuration
- **Parameters:** Base MLP has 8 layers of 512 hidden units. Static and Transient/Uncertainty MLPs have 4 layers of 128 hidden units each. Positional encoding frequencies are 15 for position and 4 for viewing direction. Sampling points are 512 per ray per model (coarse and fine) during training (1024 total), doubled to 2048 during evaluation. Appearance embedding dimension $n(a) = 48$. Transient object embedding dimension $n(\tau) = 16$. L1 regularizer multiplier $\lambda_u = 0.01$. Minimum importance threshold $\beta_{min} = 0.03$. Optimizer is Adam, batch size 2048, initial learning rate 0.001, decaying ten-fold every 150,000 iterations, over 300,000 iterations total [S3].
- **Number:** Hyperparameters were optimized for the Brandenburg Gate scene of the Phototourism dataset and reused for remaining scenes [S3].

### Explicit Mesh Reconstruction from Neural Fields
- **Definition:** An algorithm to extract an explicit 3D mesh representation from the implicit neural radiance field learned by CodeNeRF, allowing for 3D reconstruction from a single input image [S4].
- **Steps:** Feed the center coordinates of a $256^3$ voxel grid to the CodeNeRF MLP to obtain volume density values $\sigma$. Apply the Marching Cubes algorithm to the volume density values $\sigma$ to find mesh vertices. Cast rays along the vertex normals of the generated mesh to associate colors to the vertices [S4].

### Efficient EndoNeRF scene representation
- **Definition:** A voxel-grids-based scene representation that replaces coordinate-based MLPs with explicit density and feature volume grids to accelerate optimization, combined with a canonical field and time-dependent deformation field for dynamic surgical scenes [S5].
- **Steps:** The dynamic scene at time $t$ is modeled by warping a canonical radiance field (represented by $\mathbf{V}_\sigma$ and $\mathbf{V}_a$) with a time-dependent deformation field. The deformation field is modeled using decomposed 4D motion fields and a 3-layer MLP that maps a spatial-temporal coordinate to a deformation offset [S5].

### NeRF-Liif
- **Definition:** A baseline method that super-resolves LR images using a pretrained LIIF (Local Implicit Image Function) model, which requires LR-HR pairs for training and introduces external data priors [S6].
- **Parameters:** Training data requirement is LR-HR pairs [S6].
- **Pitfalls:** On synthetic Blender dataset, LIIF may produce false predictions due to domain mismatch with its external training set. On real-world LLFF dataset, LIIF tends to be oversmooth and may predict false color or geometry [S6].
- **Number:** Blender ×2 (100x100): PSNR 27.07, SSIM 0.919, LPIPS 0.067. Blender ×4 (100x100): PSNR 25.36, SSIM 0.885, LPIPS 0.125. Blender ×2 (200x200): PSNR 28.81, SSIM 0.934, LPIPS 0.058. Blender ×4 (200x200): PSNR 27.34, SSIM 0.912, LPIPS 0.096. LLFF ×2: PSNR 26.81, SSIM 0.823, LPIPS 0.145. LLFF ×4: PSNR 24.76, SSIM 0.723, LPIPS 0.292 [S6].

### UniSurf
- **Definition:** A method unifying volume rendering (radiance fields) and surface rendering (implicit surfaces) to achieve high-quality geometry and sharp textures without mask supervision [S7, unofficial].
- **Steps:** Uses an occupancy field where the occupancy at the $i^{th}$ sample corresponds to an indicator of surface presence. Uses volume rendering in the early stage for optimization without mask supervision. Uses surface rendering in the later stage to extract level-set surfaces [S7, unofficial].
- **Comparison:** Unlike pure surface rendering which requires mask supervision and has blurry texture mapping, this method provides high-quality novel views and sharp textures/colors without mask supervision [S7, unofficial].

## Background
The foundational NeRF architecture [15] introduced the use of MLPs with positional encoding for coordinate-based radiance fields. Subsequent works have explored various modifications to improve rendering quality, training speed, and representation efficiency. NeRF-W [S3] extended this to unconstrained photo collections. Instant-NGP [S1] introduced multi-resolution hash encoding for real-time training. Mip-NeRF [S1] addressed aliasing through integrated positional encoding. BiRF [S1] explored binary constraints for storage efficiency. SUDS [S1] extended the representation to 4D dynamic scenes. CCNeRF [S1] utilized tensor decompositions for compression. Rip-NeRF [S1] introduced anisotropic Gaussian representations. UE4-NeRF [S1] integrated NeRFs into game engines. GOF [S1] unified occupancy and radiance fields for generative modeling. Panoptic Radiance Field [S1] added semantic and instance understanding. Frequency-Modulated Position Encoding [S1] adapted encodings for point clouds. Triplane NeRF with Diffusion Prior [S1] combined triplane representations with diffusion models. EG3D [S2] used triplanes for 3D-aware GANs. CodeNeRF [S4] enabled mesh extraction. Efficient EndoNeRF [S5] used voxel grids for surgical scenes. NeRF-Liif [S6] applied super-resolution. UniSurf [S7, unofficial] unified surface and volume rendering.
